title: Weston v. Cassata
lead: Welfare recipients challenge recurring sanction notices, and the county’s reliance on “no entitlement” language fails because available funds and mandatory eligibility rules already constrain its treatment of current participants.

actors.name: Frances Weston, Christine Kneubehl, and Shauna Disher
actors.role: Class representatives sanctioned under Colorado Works.

actors.name: Adams County department director and social-services board
actors.role: Officials responsible for administering benefits and notices; appellants.

actors.name: Colorado state department
actors.role: Developed forms and sanction codes; state defendants were outside this appeal.

proceedings: After a bench trial, the trial court declared five notice versions inadequate, enjoined them, ordered prior sanctions reversed and records removed, and directed restoration.
The Colorado Court of Appeals affirmed on July 5, 2001.
limits: The protected interest was conditional continued benefits for eligible recipients while funds were available, not perpetual appropriations. The appeal did not quantify individual damages or fees. Denver defendants had settled, and state defendants were not parties to this appeal.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Welfare reform assigns counties responsibility for conditional benefits
sections.cue: What must happen before sanctions reduce assistance?
paragraphs: The federal Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 replaced Aid to Families with Dependent Children with Temporary Assistance for Needy Families. It used conditional state block grants and a sixty-month limit for eligible adult caregivers. Colorado adopted its Works Program in 1997, requiring individual responsibility contracts and allowing reduced cash assistance for noncompliance.

Before sanctions, the county had to explain the basis and the route to a county conference or state appeal. The state department developed forms and sanction codes, but counties completed and delivered adverse-action notices. Adams County’s assigned distribution and administration duties remained despite state oversight.

Frances Weston, Christine Kneubehl, and Shauna Disher represented sanctioned recipients. They sued the county director and social-services board under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, Colorado’s Administrative Procedure Act, and declaratory-judgment law, requesting declarations, an injunction, reversed sanctions, restored benefits, and § 1988 fees. Denver defendants settled, and state defendants were outside this appeal.

sources.pinpoint: 37 P.3d at 472–474; Welfare reform; Parties and setting

sections.title: Five notice versions fail at a bench trial
sections.cue: What judgment did the county appeal?
paragraphs: After trial, the court found none of five versions used between July 1997 and November 1999 met legal notice requirements. All omitted sanction amounts and sufficiently specific reasons. Early forms also failed to explain later benefit effects, identify governing rules, and give the proper appeal time, listing twenty-six instead of ninety days. Later versions fixed some items, eventually including a missing rollover date, but retained central defects.

The trial court declared the notices inadequate, barred further use, ordered reversal and removal of earlier sanction records based on them, and directed equitable restoration of improperly withheld cash assistance. The county appealed. Judge Davidson wrote for Judges Metzger and Roy, reviewing statutory interpretation anew.

The county said it was not a § 1983 “person.” The court distinguished exclusions involving States and some official-capacity damages suits from prospective declaratory and injunctive proceedings against implementing officials. These administrators were proper defendants for the relief at issue; state authorship of forms did not excuse their own duties.

sources.pinpoint: 37 P.3d at 473–474, 478–479; Procedural setting; County responsibility

sections.title: The court reads mandatory payment duties alongside “no entitlement” clauses
sections.cue: Why did the disclaimers not eliminate all property interests?
paragraphs: Under Roth’s property framework, due process required a legitimate entitlement grounded in independent law rather than need alone. Federal language denied individual entitlement under funded state programs, and Colorado likewise disclaimed a legal entitlement. The court accepted that reform changed the prior system but rejected reading those sentences to erase all other statutory commands.

Subject to appropriations, a participant “shall” receive a basic grant; benefits continued during appeal; and adverse actions required written notice. Those duties had to be reconciled with the disclaimer. The court distinguished an absolute benefit guarantee, fiscal commitments to fund programs, and property interests arising when substantive standards constrained discretion within an operating program.

Government retained funding choices, and federal authorities could withhold grants from noncompliant States. Before money became available, expectations had not matured. But with funds present, eligibility met, and payments begun, the county lacked discretion to withhold for reasons outside statutory criteria. Officials conceded that duty.

Barry differed because officials retained choices among eligible shelter applicants. The court used Professor Farina’s explanation that due process protected accurate application of criteria after a grant, not benefit receipt under every circumstance. Loudermill likewise prevented the legislature from creating protected property while removing constitutionally adequate deprivation procedures. Current recipients therefore held a conditional interest; funding limits remained.

sources.pinpoint: 37 P.3d at 474–477; Property-interest dispute; Conditional funding

sections.title: Meaningful notice requires enough detail to contest the actual sanction
sections.cue: Which omissions made the process inadequate?
paragraphs: The county invoked Goldberg’s timely-and-adequate-notice principle. Applicable regulations specified understandable action and reasons, legal authority, effective dates, review routes and deadlines, continuation and repayment consequences, representation rights, and where practicable the recipient’s language, with oral explanation for illiteracy.

The proven omissions materially failed those standards. Recipients could not meaningfully contest an unspecified sanction amount and vague reason, and early incorrect deadlines further impaired review. The appellate court found the trial findings supported and sustained the due-process ruling. It did not declare every harmless typographical defect unconstitutional.

sections.title: Individual restorations fail to correct the system, making exhaustion unnecessary here
sections.cue: Why did administrative appeal not offer the relief this class sought?
paragraphs: The county argued lack of exhaustion deprived the trial court of authority over state claims. The evidence showed routine restoration when recipients appealed while the same flawed notices continued. Officials refused revision even after administrative findings of inadequacy. Individual restorations ended particular disputes without review of the ongoing notice practice.

The administrative framework handled individual benefit decisions and could not supply the classwide correction sought. Futility and practices avoiding judicial review therefore excused exhaustion on this record, not in every benefits case seeking broad relief.

On July 5, 2001, the Colorado Court of Appeals affirmed the notice injunction, reversal and record-removal directions, and equitable restoration. It set no individual damages sum or fee award. No separate opinion appeared. The judgment protected accurate application of existing eligibility rules without promising funding or assistance forever.

sources.pinpoint: 37 P.3d at 478–479; Exhaustion; Decision and limits
